author: Kit Kittelstad
title: The Most Beautiful Churches and Cathedrals in Paris - NewsBreak
text: Paris might be well-known for its pastries, fashion, and romantic streets, but we can’t overlook the history that lies within its churches and cathedrals. Whether you’re a history buff, architecture nerd, or just in it for some spectacular photos, these sacred spots are worth a detour (or an entire day). We’ve visited the City of Light many times and gathered up our list of the most beautiful churches and cathedrals in Paris, each with its own personality and story. We hope, the next time you’re there, you’ll step inside one or two. In some instances, you’ll feel the atmosphere shift and find it a welcome reprieve from the hustle and bustle of one of Europe’s most fascinating cities. Tucked away behind the Panthéon, Saint-Étienne-du-Mont is one of those places you could easily miss – but please don’t. It’s stunning inside, with a unique rood screen (a sort of stone balcony) that you’ll rarely see in other churches. The blend of Gothic and Renaissance styles makes it feel like you stepped into a living piece of art. In addition to all that rare beauty, fans of Midnight in Paris will also recognize the steps outside where Owen Wilson’s character gets whisked back in time to meet the likes of Ernest Hemingway, F. Scott Fitzgerald, and Gertrude Stein. Inside, be sure to seek out the shrine of Saint Geneviève, the patron saint of Paris, to admire the gorgeous stained glass. All in all, Saint-Étienne is a peaceful, under-the-radar gem that we hope you’ll add to the top of your list. The only way to describe Sainte-Chapelle is to say it’s like walking into a kaleidoscope. Built in the 13th century by Louis IX to house his collection of Passion relics (including the Crown of Thorns), it’s all about the stained glass here. There are 15 huge windows that tell over a thousand biblical stories. The chapel itself isn’t very big, but the effect is massive. Sunlight pours through the colored glass and paints the whole room in hues of reds, blues, and purples. It’s breathtaking, especially if you catch it on a sunny day. If you visit Paris during the high season (June to August, and December), the line to get in can be quite long. So, if you can, try to book ahead. Right near Les Halles, Saint-Eustache will truly surprise you. Mixing Gothic architecture with Renaissance detailing, it somehow feels both grand and intimate at the same time. When you visit, you might hear someone practicing on the pipe organ, one of the largest in France. Saint-Eustache has a storied past. Louis XIV received his First Holy Communion here, and Mozart chose it for his mother’s funeral. The church is also known for supporting the arts, so you could even stumble upon a concert or installation. Trust us when we say Saint-Eustache is an experience unto itself. If you’ve read The Da Vinci Code , you probably already know a little about Saint-Sulpice. It’s Paris’s second-largest church, and the interior is full of surprises. Check out the huge Delacroix murals, especially in the Chapel of the Holy Angels. They’re dramatic and full of movement. The church also has a fascinating gnomon (a scientific instrument that tracks the sun) and a beautifully restored pipe organ. The façade is a bit quirky because of its uneven towers, but that just adds to its charm. A good word for Saint-Sulpice is multi-faceted; it has stories to tell if you hang around long enough. Here come two heavy-hitters. We’ll start with the one that requires a bit of a walk. Perched on top of Montmartre, Sacré-Cœur looks like a sugar-coated dream. It was built in the late 1800s as a symbol of hope after the Franco-Prussian War and, now, it’s one of Paris’s most iconic sights. Inside, the ceiling mosaic of Christ in Majesty is one of the largest in the world and absolutely mesmerizing. Sadly, photos are not allowed; it’ll just have to live on in your heart forever. Also, don’t skip the dome; you can climb up it for one of the most panoramic views of the city. The area around it is charming, too, particularly Place du Tertre, with all the artists painting in the square and plenty of cafés for a sip of wine. And, if you have food on your mind, here are ten more unforgettable things to see, do, and eat in Paris. Here’s one we all know and love. This Gothic masterpiece has been the soul of Paris for centuries. The rose windows, the gargoyles, the flying buttresses – they’re all part of the magic. After the devastating fire in 2019, Notre-Dame went through a major restoration and just reopened in 2024. It’s heartwarming to see it standing tall and proud again, with many of its beloved features restored, including the iconic spire. If you’d like to visit, online reservations are recommended (so you can skip the lines). Graciously, it’s still free to get in. Those reservations are just a suggestion because, to no surprise, the demand to get in remains high, especially after being closed for five years. Built in the 19th century, Sainte Marie-Madeleine, or La Madeleine, is smack dab in the middle of some very chic shopping streets. And, if you didn’t know any better, you might mistake it for a Greek temple. This pretty lady showcases massive Corinthian columns and a neoclassical design that sets it apart from the rest. Inside, it feels surprisingly cozy, compared to its imposing exterior. There’s a quiet sense of grandeur, with beautiful sculptures and a golden altar that catches the light just right. Aside from a quick stop-by on your rambles, you might want to keep your eye on its calendar of events . Some lovely classical music concerts are hosted here, and the acoustics are divine. Welcome to the oldest church in Paris. Saint-Germain-des-Prés dates back to the 6th century, and stepping inside certainly feels like stepping back in time. It’s gone through many renovations, but parts of the original structure still remain. This church is deeply tied to the philosophical side of Paris. It’s right near the famous Café de Flore and Les Deux Magots. (Hemingway loved writing in both spots.) Inside, you’ll find beautiful frescoes and a peaceful atmosphere that offers a lovely break from the moving streets of Paris. This one’s a bit off the beaten path, tucked away on one of the quieter islands. Église Saint-Louis-en-l’Île is small but elegant, with a restrained baroque style that feels very Parisian. What makes it special is the intimacy. It’s not usually packed with tourists, so you can actually sit, breathe, and take in the details, like the soft light filtering through the windows or the polished wood and stone. Here, too, you’ll also find beautiful classical concerts, which feel extra special in such a quiet setting. On Île Saint-Louis, you’ll also find one of our favorite cafes: Saint-Régis. It’s featured in our solo guide to Paris and is worth a little linger after you visit this lovely church. A bit outside of central Paris, Basílica de Saint-Denis is worth the short trip. This is where French kings and queens are buried, and it’s often considered the first true Gothic building in the city. The stained glass here is magnificent, and the royal tombs are unlike anything you’ll see anywhere else in the city. In truth, it feels ike a museum and a church in one, which probably isn’t too far off the mark for any of the churches on this list. Like Église Saint-Louis-en-l’Île, it doesn’t get the same crowds as Notre-Dame or Sacré-Cœur, so you can really soak it all in. Whether you’re lighting a candle, snapping a few photos, or just soaking in the serenity, Paris’s churches and cathedrals open the door to a completely different kind of beauty. Each one is a window into the city’s soul. As you visit some of these gems, take the time to explore. Your favorite might be one you hadn’t even heard of yet. To help you plan your Parisian trip to perfection, including where to stay, where to eat, and a slew of sites that only locals know about, come check out our library of destination guides . We’re here to help you navigate everything from Paris’ arrondissements to Barcelona’s barrios. And, the next time we visit one of these beauties, we’ll be sure to light a candle for you.
